rationale: A wins because it gives four legitimately different desks a usable story, then tells the founder what proof would make each survive assignment. Its "An unprofitable automaker turns its charging network into a revenue line" is the clean business story; B's "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates — the loyalty math of a shared network" is a softer rewrap of the same premium-pricing fact, not a fresh assignment. A has one bad headline-level overclaim, but B pads the premium fact into two angles and leaves the standards story underbuilt.
gaps_in_A: "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over" overstates the fact. One Rivian connector decision does not prove the connector fight is over.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners" may be true, but it is not in the update. Source it or soften it.

"operators eating the hardware cost of supporting both standards" is plausible infrastructure analysis, not a supplied fact. The angle correctly asks for cost proof, but the body still gets ahead of the evidence.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates — the loyalty math of a shared network" duplicates "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own." Same premium-pricing fact, two envelopes.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" smuggles in an unnamed competitor comparison that the update does not support.

"Tesla Supercharger access, Electrify America, the NACS transition" may be the right context, but B invokes it without a supplied peg or source. That is where sloppy pitches start wearing a trade-reporter costume.
B misses a real standalone standards angle from "all new stalls will include both CCS and Tesla-style NACS connectors," then refuses the NACS idea instead of shaping it properly.
